text.content:
As legend has it, Caine himself passed the Traditions down to his childer in the time of the First City to guide them through their unlives. To this day they remain the bulwark of @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.sects.JournalEntry.fc464242d84d4e34]{Camarilla} society and are strictly upheld — not out of blind reverence, but because they make good practical sense for a species of secret predators. Within the Camarilla, every other rule, ordinance, and custom is understood as an interpretation of or elaboration on these six laws.

The First Tradition: The Masquerade

"Thou shalt not reveal thy true nature to those not of the Blood. Doing so shall renounce thy claims of Blood."

Most Camarilla Kindred consider this the whole of the law, and everything else incidental. Over the five centuries since the Inquisition's madness and slaughter, the Kindred have worked hardest at eradicating belief in vampires: squashing reports, discrediting or eliminating witnesses, and disciplining perpetrators. The mistakes that led to the Inquisition are ruthlessly punished in memory. Breaching the Masquerade — through violence, careless use of powers, or simply talking too freely — is most often answered with death.

The Second Tradition: Domain

"Thy domain is thy concern. All others owe thee respect while in it. None may challenge thy word in thy domain."

As available territory has shrunk over the centuries, it has become rare for any vampire who holds significant domain not to also be a prince; more often a prince parcels out portions of his domain in payment for service, expecting the occupant to enforce his will in exchange rather than to act with true autonomy. Some modern-minded Kindred have begun asserting "domain" over commercial or digital territory (brokerage firms, software companies) rather than city blocks, a trend elders tend to dismiss.

The Third Tradition: Progeny

"Thou shalt sire another only with the permission of thine elder. If thou createst another without thine elder's leave, both thou and thy progeny shall be slain."

As princes came to replace sires as the practical meaning of "elder," the right to create childer became one of the most jealously guarded princely prerogatives. Siring without permission is a capital offense for both sire and childe.

The Fourth Tradition: Accounting

"Those thou create are thine own childer. Until thy progeny are released, thou shalt command them in all things. Their sins are thine to endure."

A sire is responsible for a new childe's actions — all of them — until the childe is formally released (typically via presentation to the prince). Any punishment for a wayward neonate's transgressions falls on sire and childe alike. Childer presented before they're ready, and found ignorant of Kindred protocol under a prince's questioning or through their own later missteps, can bring severe punishment down on both themselves and their sires.

The Fifth Tradition: Hospitality

"Honor one another's domain. When thou comest to a foreign city, thou shalt present thyself to the one who ruleth there. Without the word of acceptance, thou art nothing."

A Kindred entering another's territory is expected to announce himself — in practice, to present himself to the local prince as soon as possible, ideally the same night he arrives — to prevent unnecessary bloodshed between predators sharing a hunting ground. Ignorance of how to make contact or of proper etiquette is never accepted as an excuse. Some vampires (the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.zCWdD1NpOCn03CwE]{Gangrel} notably among them) flout this Tradition and get away with it only by keeping a low enough profile; scourges exist chiefly to hunt down the unpresented.

The Sixth Tradition: Destruction

"Thou art forbidden to destroy another of thy kind. The right of destruction belongeth only to thine elder. Only the eldest among thee shall call the blood hunt."

Originally a sire's right over an unruly childe, this Tradition's authority has been almost entirely usurped by the prince in modern nights: a sire retains free rein to destroy a fractious childe only up until that childe's presentation, after which the childe becomes the property of the city rather than of the sire. The right to destroy any presented, acknowledged vampire belongs solely to the prince; anyone who takes that right into his own hands can expect to become the target of a blood hunt himself. This Tradition also covers diablerie, treated as the ultimate violation. The threat of the blood hunt, used prudently, is one of a prince's most powerful tools; used capriciously, it can bring down her entire reign.
